title: Europe’s Geoeconomic Predicament
text:
← Back to Projects


Why is industrial policy en vogue in the European Union? The fear of falling behind has long driven European integration, but the answer used to be more market creation. Given the EU’s market-making impetus, its tilt toward fiscal austerity, and its limits on state aid, the recent turn to directing economic activity is surprising. I have traced how the geopoliticization of trade gave neo-mercantilist and socially oriented actors an opening to challenge Europe’s embedded neoliberal compromise, and how the Commission took on a far more active role in the name of technological sovereignty.
How this works on the ground is another matter. The conditions attached to the EU’s flagship subsidies, the Important Projects of Common European Interest, bring perverse outcomes, adverse selection, and workarounds: one chipmaker had to throw away a perfectly good test batch, because selling it would have counted as mass production. Outcomes are decided where firms meet instruments, so my current work turns to the firms themselves. In 2022, Annalena Baerbock warned business elites that they “cannot afford to act following a ‘business first’ mantra alone.” Which firms back European sovereignty in what they do as well as in what they say? Are they patriots, or profiteurs?




Papers
Patriots or Profiteurs? (with R. Bosticco). Paper in progress. Explains how firms respond, economically and politically, to sovereignty-seeking policy in semiconductors and batteries.
The Costs of Conditionality (with T. Seidl and T. Wuttke). Competition & Change, 2026. Examines how the EU’s flagship industrial policy works on the ground.
Picking Losers (with T. Ergen). Regulation & Governance, 2025. Documents how decarbonization drew the EU into managing decline in targeted regions and sectors.
Moving On to Not Fall Behind? (with T. Seidl). Journal of European Public Policy, 2024. Reconstructs the “geo-dirigiste” turn through Europe’s fear of falling behind. JEPP Best Paper Prize 2024.
Europe First? (with D. Di Carlo). Journal of European Public Policy, 2023. Charts the rise of an EU industrial policy that promotes and protects the single market.
As Open as Possible, as Autonomous as Necessary (with T. Seidl). Journal of Common Market Studies, 2023. Shows how the Commission used open strategic autonomy as a coalition magnet.
When External Pressures Shift Domestic Coalitions (with J. Simons). Manuscript available upon request. Traces the Dutch shift from horizontal orthodoxy through covert verticalism to overt interventionism.
Whose Strategic Autonomy? (with D. Karas). Manuscript available upon request. Asks whether integration leaves Ukraine a raw-material supplier or moves it up the value chain.

title: Europe’s Geoeconomic Predicament
text:
The Challenge to Market-Based Governance
Why is industrial policy en vogue in the European Union? Given the EU’s market-making impetus, tilt towards fiscal austerity, and limits to subsidizing state aid, the turn to an active and targeted industrial policy in the last years is surprising. I argue that a declining belief in open markets and economic efficiency as the sole propagators of ‘good’ economic outcomes has mobilized a coalition of firms, business associations, and trade unions to challenge the EU’s market-based governance regime.

title: Europe’s Geoeconomic Predicament
text:
Manifestations
This is visible in EU trade policy, now understood in terms of open strategic autonomy, and especially visible in digital and high-tech fields and in the green transition, often discussed under the rubric of the ‘twin transitions’.

title: Luuk Schmitz
text:
Hello! I am a senior researcher at the Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies (MPIfG) in Cologne. I hold a PhD in political and social science from the European University Institute with a dissertation on European industrial policy.
My research deals with the political economy of geoeconomics. I am interested in how multinational firms operate under geoeconomic tensions, how geoeconomics reshape trade and investment patterns, and how this affects decarbonization and the green transition. Geographically, I focus mostly on the European Union. Additionally, I have an interest in computational social science, and how we can bridge the gap between linguistics, computer science, and political science.
You can find more information about my research, publications, and contact info on this website. I occasionally post miscellaneous entries in my blog on more general academic interests.

title: Changing the Calculus on Economic Security
text:
← Back to Projects


Tariffs come and go like weather; geopolitics has become the climate. Since 2022 it has settled into what firms tell their investors, and it has stayed there long after the instruments that first brought it up have faded. This project asks what firms do with that new climate. Some bear it as a cost and others pocket a windfall. A third group claims a calling, presenting its capacity as indispensable to projects of resilience, sovereignty, and security. States answered such claims early, whereas investors paid for them only once the United States showed, in April 2025, that it would reorder markets around geopolitical priorities.
When the Pentagon took a stake that would make it MP Materials’ largest shareholder, guaranteed a price for its rare earths, and committed to buy every magnet from its new plant, there was still a buyer, a seller, and a price. Yet is that a market? Corporate power, on this view, does not simply rise or fall. Rather, it moves toward firms that can make themselves part of the project, on terms neither side fully controls.




Papers
The Geopolitical Construction of Markets. Manuscript available upon request. Traces how claims of necessity become durable participation in state projects.
Hierarchies of Adaptation. OSF Preprint, 2026. An earlier version of the argument.

title: Changing the Calculus on Economic Security
text:
Core Research Question
The core intuition behind the project is to place (real or imagined) security imperatives center stage. The aim of this project is to find out how such imperatives increasingly shape economic policy interventions, as well as corporate decision-making. We currently lack the theoretical and methodological toolkit to tackle such questions.
After several decades of intensifying globalization, the world has entered a new phase centered around geoeconomic fragmentation. Terms such as de-globalization, decoupling, and de-risking have entered public discourse and corporate reports, and increasingly shape policy interventions as governments vie to position themselves in a geopoliticizing world. An economic view centered around efficiency and factor endowment increasingly struggles to explain the security-based choices forced on firms and markets by states. From an efficiency-based point of view, replicating entire value chains within national borders is a form of economic downgrading. If so, why does this happen?

title: Changing the Calculus on Economic Security
text:
Methodology
The project goes beyond the usual ‘supply-side’ bias in the literature, which has so far mostly analyzed policy documents and individual companies. I have collected an original data set of corporate earnings calls (n=20.014) that involves more than 4500 companies and spans eight years (starting in 2016). The large number of firms allows for a large-scale and nuanced analysis of how geoeconomic competition affects firms and sectors across time.

title: Changing the Calculus on Economic Security
text:
Research Goals
In a first step, I aim to map theoretically and empirically what such an economic ‘calculus’ is, and how it is changing. In a follow-up paper, I want to analyze who are the winners and losers of geoeconomic competition.

title: Mesonomics: Rescaling Political Economy
text:
← Back to Projects


Go looking for the great decoupling in the trade aggregates and it tends to disappear in oceans of data, as flows reroute through Vietnam and Mexico rather than collapse. Go looking inside a single firm and everything seems to have changed. Political economists have long bet on one resolution or the other, which Thomas Oatley called the reductionist gamble. Yet the action now sits in between, in the supply chains, ownership networks, and investment circuits through which states and firms reach one another.
Mesonomics is my effort to build instruments for that middle layer. The core is a thermometer for corporate activity: 46,348 earnings calls held by 9,450 firms since 2016, read with language models validated against hand coding, and linked to some 766,000 buyer-seller ties, share prices, lobbying records, and tariff petitions. This lets me set what firms claim against what they hold, what investors pay for, and what states give.




Resources
A Primer for the Use of Classifier and Generative Large Language Models in Social Science Research (with J. Cova). OSF Preprint, 2024. A practical guide, with replication materials.
The earnings-call and supply-chain database underpins Changing the Calculus on Economic Security and The Politics of Fracture.

title: Mesonomics: Rescaling Political Economy
text:
The Reductionist Gamble
A major challenge for comparative and international political economists is the discrepancy between the behavior of statistical aggregates and individual agents. Our theories and methods of accounting remain separated between macro-institutional processes and micro-level outcomes that focus on individual firms, organizations, and sectors. To assume away complexity by ignoring one or the other is to engage in what Thomas Oatley has called the reductionist gamble.

title: Mesonomics: Rescaling Political Economy
text:
The Need for Meso-Level Analysis
With the advent of economic statecraft and the weaponization of markets for geopolitical purposes comes an urgent need to understand how states and firms interact across markets, supply chains, and financial networks. The discovery of such meso-level processes has been labeled mesonomics.

title: Mesonomics: Rescaling Political Economy
text:
Current Applications
The more widespread availability of firm-level data and the computational methods to analyze them now allows political economists to get more serious about addressing these questions. In my current work, firm-level data plays a major role. Apart from the economic calculus project outlined above, I use data on the automobile industry to map the geographical dispersion and organization of car makers’ supply chains.

title: Stacking Order
text:
← Back to Projects


If Cold War I was about clashing modernities, Cold War II is about clashing techno-economic regimes. This book argues that the origins of the geoeconomic turn lie less in state strategy than in changing corporate planning routines. The complexity, capital intensity, and input scarcity of contemporary production, from AI infrastructure to clean energy systems and semiconductor fabs, have outgrown what price-driven markets can coordinate. Firms have responded by bundling physical resources, technical protocols, and industrial ecosystems into walled gardens that serve equally well to capture rents as to enclose geopolitical space.
The book unfolds in three acts: authoring the stack through long-term planning, expanding it abroad, and controlling the terms on which its capabilities spread. Where Thomas Hughes showed how technological systems acquire momentum through time, stacked interdependence shows how geopolitical actors now engineer momentum through space. The central political question of the 2020s is therefore not market versus state, but which forms of non-market coordination prevail, who controls them, and whether democratic societies can govern them.

title: Stacking Order
text:
From Flows to Stacks
What does global interdependence look like in a multipolar world? For decades, globalization has reshaped political rule, economic arrangements, social relationships, and cultural forms. A political order backed by American centrality in commerce, finance, technology, and defense fostered an economic order where markets opened, supply chains sprawled, and governance technocratized. The breakdown of this order coincides with a time of profound economic transformation. This book argues that the origin of this shift lies not in state strategy, but in changing corporate planning routines: the complexity and capital intensity of contemporary production (AI infrastructure, clean energy systems, semiconductor fabs) has outgrown the coordination capacity of price-driven markets. These firms responded by vertically integrating supply chains, locking in standards, and building planning infrastructures that bundle physical resources, technical protocols, and industrial ecosystems into cohesive architectures of control. The walled gardens this creates serve equally well to increase profits as to enclose geopolitical space. By consequence, the grammar of geopolitical conflict revolves around which of these architectures their economies are wired into. Therefore, this book argues that the relevant political question in the 2020s isn’t market vs. state but rather which forms of non-market coordination prevail, who controls them, and whether democratic societies can govern them.

title: Corporate Planning and Grand Strategy
text:
← Back to Projects


For thirty years, the leading firm owned little and orchestrated much, using the market to discipline its suppliers. The technologies of the twin transition do not come apart so neatly. A battery, a chassis, and its software have to be designed together; an AI data center works as one machine. Firms therefore bring production back in-house, as BYD has, or lock in their futures through long contracts, as the hyperscalers have with memory and power. Galbraith’s planning system is back, and Hirschman tells us why: every bottleneck calls forth a plan.
Yet a plan also allocates, and the currency of power becomes entry into it. Those inside receive certainty, while consoles and MRI scanners queue for memory and households for the grid. Who holds the pen differs, too: in the United States, firms tend to move first and enlist the state and finance along the way, whereas in China the state sets the direction and firms carry it abroad. With four American firms now committing some two percent of US GDP a year, that is a political question of the first order.




Papers
Planning the Tech-Industrial Complex (with L. Dagorne). Under review. Shows how long-term contracts establish priority claims on future capacity, and why Washington underwrites them.
Vertical Integration in the Electric Vehicle Revolution (with P. Gerbaudo and G. Anzolin). Manuscript available upon request. Compares BYD and Tesla with Toyota and Volkswagen.
What Is Different About Chinese Automotive Capitalism? (with P. Polyak). Paper in progress. Shows how integration, demand pressures, and geopolitical steering combine to carry industrial stacks abroad.

title: The Politics of Fracture
text:
← Back to Projects


In 2018, the electrical-equipment maker Eaton filed more than sixty requests to exempt its imports from American steel tariffs, each for itself alone. Three years later, it lobbied for clean-energy credits through a lobbying firm it shared with a power producer, an offshore-wind developer, and a biofuels company. Our theories of trade politics do not predict this switch, because they were built for liberalization, when value chains were the scaffolding of coalitions.
This project traces what becomes of business politics when geoeconomics arrives as restriction, as reward, or as shock. Restrictions offer relief that each firm claims for itself, so steelmakers end up objecting to the exemptions of their own customers. Inducements create programs that must be won and defended together. Shocks without an instrument behind them mobilize no one, because politics needs an address. Distributive conflict thus cuts through sectors rather than between them. Whose interest, then, is “the European car industry’s”?




Papers
Exit, Coalitions, and Anomy: Business Politics under Geoeconomics. Paper in progress. Links exposure in earnings calls to federal lobbying disclosures, tariff-relief petitions, and firm-to-firm supply-chain networks.
